notes.front: Which businesses does the Virginia Consumer Data Protection Act cover?
notes.back: Those in or targeting Virginia that process data of 100,000 consumers, or of 25,000 while earning over half their revenue from selling data.
notes.explanation: The 100,000 test is counted per calendar year.
notes.source: Code of Virginia, title 59.1, chapter 53 (Consumer Data Protection Act), § 59.1-576(A)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What are two kinds of organisation that the Virginia Consumer Data Protection Act does not apply to?
notes.back: Any two of: state and local government bodies; GLBA financial institutions; HIPAA covered entities and business associates; nonprofits; higher education institutions.
notes.explanation: These are exemptions of whole organisations, not only of particular data.
notes.source: Code of Virginia, title 59.1, chapter 53 (Consumer Data Protection Act), § 59.1-576(B)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A company processes data of 30,000 Virginia consumers and earns 60 per cent of its gross revenue from selling personal data. Is it covered by the VCDPA?
notes.back: A: Yes: at least 25,000 consumers and over 50 per cent of revenue from selling data.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, under the 25,000 consumers and 50 per cent test
B) No, it needs 100,000 consumers
C) No, Virginia has a revenue threshold of 25 million dollars
D) Only if it has an office in Virginia
notes.choicesExplained: B: 100,000 is the alternative test. C: that is California's style of test, not Virginia's. D: targeting Virginia residents is enough.
notes.explanation: The smaller consumer count is enough when combined with the revenue test.
notes.source: Code of Virginia, title 59.1, chapter 53 (Consumer Data Protection Act), § 59.1-576(A)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A Virginia employer holds its staff's personnel records. Do the employees have VCDPA rights over those records as 'consumers'?
notes.back: C: No: the VCDPA's consumer excludes people acting in an employment context.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, all residents are consumers
B) Yes, but only the right to delete
C) No, people acting in an employment context are excluded
D) Only if the employer sells the records
notes.choicesExplained: A and B: the definition excludes the employment context. D: the exclusion does not depend on sale.
notes.explanation: The definition is limited to individual or household contexts.
notes.source: Code of Virginia, title 59.1, chapter 53 (Consumer Data Protection Act), § 59.1-575
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What are three rights a consumer has under the Virginia Consumer Data Protection Act?
notes.back: Any three of: confirm and access; correct; delete; obtain a portable copy; opt out of targeted advertising, sale or significant profiling.
notes.explanation: The consumer invokes them by a request to the controller, which must comply with an authenticated request.
notes.source: Code of Virginia, title 59.1, chapter 53 (Consumer Data Protection Act), § 59.1-577(A)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A Virginia consumer learns that a lender uses automated profiling to decide her loan applications. Which VCDPA right lets her stop this processing?
notes.back: D: The right to opt out of profiling in furtherance of decisions with legal or similarly significant effects.
notes.choices:
A) The right to delete
B) The right to correct
C) The right to data portability
D) The right to opt out of significant profiling
notes.choicesExplained: A, B and C: these rights concern the data itself, not stopping profiling for significant decisions.
notes.explanation: Decisions on financial and lending services are among those with legal or similarly significant effects.
notes.source: Code of Virginia, title 59.1, chapter 53 (Consumer Data Protection Act), § 59.1-577(A)(5) and 59.1-575
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How quickly must a Virginia controller respond to a consumer rights request?
notes.back: Without undue delay and within 45 days, extendable once by 45 days if the consumer is told within the first 45.
notes.explanation: The extension must be reasonably necessary given the complexity and number of requests.
notes.source: Code of Virginia, title 59.1, chapter 53 (Consumer Data Protection Act), § 59.1-577(B)(1)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How long does a Virginia controller have to decide a consumer's appeal against refusing a request?
notes.back: 60 days from receiving the appeal, with a written explanation of its decision.
notes.explanation: If the appeal is denied, the controller must tell the consumer how to complain to the Attorney General.
notes.source: Code of Virginia, title 59.1, chapter 53 (Consumer Data Protection Act), § 59.1-577(C)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What must a Virginia controller obtain before processing a consumer's sensitive data?
notes.back: The consumer's consent; for a known child's sensitive data, processing must follow COPPA.
notes.explanation: Consent means a clear affirmative act that is freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous.
notes.source: Code of Virginia, title 59.1, chapter 53 (Consumer Data Protection Act), § 59.1-578(A)(5) and 59.1-575
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What are two categories of sensitive data under the Virginia Consumer Data Protection Act?
notes.back: Any two of: racial or ethnic origin, religion, health diagnosis or sexual orientation; identifying genetic or biometric data; a known child's data; precise geolocation.
notes.explanation: A child here means a person younger than 13.
notes.source: Code of Virginia, title 59.1, chapter 53 (Consumer Data Protection Act), § 59.1-575
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A Virginia fitness app wants to process users' mental health diagnoses to tailor coaching. What does the VCDPA require?
notes.back: D: The user's consent, since data revealing a mental health diagnosis is sensitive data.
notes.choices:
A) Only a privacy notice
B) An opt-out link
C) Approval from the Attorney General
D) The user's consent
notes.choicesExplained: A and B: notice or opt-out is not enough for sensitive data. C: the Attorney General does not approve processing.
notes.explanation: Sensitive data may not be processed without the consumer's consent.
notes.source: Code of Virginia, title 59.1, chapter 53 (Consumer Data Protection Act), § 59.1-578(A)(5)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How does Virginia's definition of 'sale of personal data' differ from the CCPA's 'sale'?
notes.back: Virginia counts only exchanges for monetary consideration; the CCPA also counts other valuable consideration.
notes.explanation: Virginia also excludes disclosures to processors, affiliates and in mergers.
notes.source: Code of Virginia, title 59.1, chapter 53 (Consumer Data Protection Act), § 59.1-575
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What are two terms the Virginia Consumer Data Protection Act requires in a controller–processor contract?
notes.back: Any two of: a duty of confidentiality for each person processing; delete or return data at the end; provide compliance information; allow assessments.
notes.explanation: The contract must also set out instructions, the nature, purpose and duration of processing, and both parties' rights and obligations.
notes.source: Code of Virginia, title 59.1, chapter 53 (Consumer Data Protection Act), § 59.1-579(B)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A shoe retailer decides to email customers offers and hires a mailing firm that sends the emails only as instructed. Under the VCDPA, what is each?
notes.back: A: The retailer is the controller; the mailing firm is the processor.
notes.choices:
A) Retailer: controller; mailing firm: processor
B) Retailer: processor; mailing firm: controller
C) Both are controllers
D) Both are third parties
notes.choicesExplained: B: the roles are reversed. C: the firm does not decide the purpose. D: the roles are controller and processor, not third parties.
notes.explanation: The retailer decides purpose and means; the firm processes on its behalf.
notes.source: Code of Virginia, title 59.1, chapter 53 (Consumer Data Protection Act), § 59.1-575
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What are three processing activities that need a Virginia data protection assessment?
notes.back: Any three of: targeted advertising; sale of personal data; risky profiling; processing sensitive data; other heightened-risk processing.
notes.explanation: Profiling needs one only where it presents a reasonably foreseeable risk of listed harms.
notes.source: Code of Virginia, title 59.1, chapter 53 (Consumer Data Protection Act), § 59.1-580(A)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Who can obtain a Virginia controller's data protection assessments, and are they public?
notes.back: The Attorney General, by civil investigative demand; the assessments stay confidential and exempt from Virginia's Freedom of Information Act.
notes.explanation: The Attorney General may evaluate them for compliance with the controller's duties.
notes.source: Code of Virginia, title 59.1, chapter 53 (Consumer Data Protection Act), § 59.1-580(D)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A Virginia controller starts showing targeted ads based on users' activity across other companies' websites. What must it do?
notes.back: C: Conduct and document a data protection assessment of that processing.
notes.choices:
A) Register with the Attorney General
B) Obtain opt-in consent from every user
C) Conduct and document a data protection assessment
D) Nothing, because ads are not sensitive
notes.choicesExplained: A: no registration exists. B: targeted advertising needs an opt-out right, not opt-in for all data. D: the assessment duty is not limited to sensitive data.
notes.explanation: Processing for targeted advertising is a listed activity needing an assessment.
notes.source: Code of Virginia, title 59.1, chapter 53 (Consumer Data Protection Act), § 59.1-580(A)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Who enforces the Virginia Consumer Data Protection Act?
notes.back: The Attorney General alone; the Act provides no private right of action.
notes.explanation: Civil penalties are up to 7,500 dollars for each violation, plus injunctions and investigation expenses.
notes.source: Code of Virginia, title 59.1, chapter 53 (Consumer Data Protection Act), § 59.1-584(A), (C), (E)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What must happen before the Virginia Attorney General can bring an action under the VCDPA?
notes.back: The AG gives 30 days' written notice; if the controller or processor cures and gives a written statement within that time, no action follows.
notes.explanation: Continued violations or breach of the written statement allow the action to proceed.
notes.source: Code of Virginia, title 59.1, chapter 53 (Consumer Data Protection Act), § 59.1-584(B)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: The Virginia Attorney General notifies a controller of a violation. Within 30 days the controller fixes it and sends a written statement that it is cured and will not recur. What happens?
notes.back: D: No action may be brought.
notes.choices:
A) The AG sues anyway for past penalties
B) The case goes to a private class action
C) The CPPA takes over
D) No action may be brought
notes.choicesExplained: A: the cure bars the action. B: there is no private right of action. C: the CPPA is a California agency.
notes.explanation: A cure plus an express written statement within the 30-day period bars an action.
notes.source: Code of Virginia, title 59.1, chapter 53 (Consumer Data Protection Act), § 59.1-584(B)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which entities does the Colorado Privacy Act cover?
notes.back: Those in or targeting Colorado that process data of 100,000 consumers a year, or of 25,000 while deriving revenue from selling data.
notes.explanation: The summary also lists exempt entities, such as state and local government and state higher education institutions.
notes.source: Colorado General Assembly, SB21-190 Protect Personal Data Privacy, bill summary (as enacted)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How does the Colorado Privacy Act's 25,000-consumer threshold differ from Virginia's?
notes.back: Colorado requires revenue from selling data with no percentage stated; Virginia requires over 50 per cent of gross revenue from selling data.
notes.explanation: Both have an alternative 100,000-consumer test.
notes.source: Colorado General Assembly, SB21-190 Protect Personal Data Privacy, bill summary (as enacted)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which rights does the Colorado Privacy Act give consumers?
notes.back: To opt out of processing; to access, correct or delete data; and to obtain a portable copy.
notes.explanation: Controllers also have duties such as purpose specification, data minimisation and care.
notes.source: Colorado General Assembly, SB21-190 Protect Personal Data Privacy, bill summary (as enacted)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A company processes data of 30,000 Colorado consumers and earns 10 per cent of its revenue from selling personal data. Is it covered by the Colorado Privacy Act?
notes.back: B: Yes: 25,000 consumers plus revenue from selling data meets the test, which sets no percentage.
notes.choices:
A) No, it needs 100,000 consumers
B) Yes, 25,000 consumers plus revenue from selling data
C) No, it needs over 50 per cent of revenue from sales
D) Only if its revenue exceeds 25 million dollars
notes.choicesExplained: A: 100,000 is the alternative test. C: that is Virginia's test. D: Colorado has no revenue floor of that kind.
notes.explanation: Under Virginia's law the same company would fall short of the 50 per cent test.
notes.source: Colorado General Assembly, SB21-190 Protect Personal Data Privacy, bill summary (as enacted)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A Colorado consumer wants to sue a company herself for breaking the Colorado Privacy Act. What does the enacted bill summary say about enforcement?
notes.back: A: Only the attorney general or district attorneys may enforce it.
notes.choices:
A) Only the attorney general or district attorneys may enforce it
B) She may sue for statutory damages
C) The CPPA handles Colorado complaints
D) Only the Federal Trade Commission may enforce it
notes.choicesExplained: B: the summary names only public enforcers. C: the CPPA is California's agency. D: this is a state law enforced by state officials.
notes.explanation: The summary limits enforcement to public enforcers.
notes.source: Colorado General Assembly, SB21-190 Protect Personal Data Privacy, bill summary (as enacted)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A controller subject to the Colorado Privacy Act asks where to find the technical specifications for the universal opt-out mechanism it must honour. Where should it look?
notes.back: B: The Colorado attorney general's rules.
notes.choices:
A) The CPPA's regulations
B) The Colorado attorney general's rules
C) The Federal Trade Commission's guidance
D) Each controller designs its own
notes.choicesExplained: A: the CPPA writes California's rules, not Colorado's. C: the FTC does not set this mechanism. D: controllers must use the mechanism the rules specify.
notes.explanation: The act requires the attorney general to adopt rules detailing the mechanism's technical specifications.
notes.source: Colorado General Assembly, SB21-190 Protect Personal Data Privacy, bill summary (as enacted)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Who sets the technical rules for California's opt-out preference signal and for Colorado's universal opt-out mechanism?
notes.back: In California, regulations adopted under the CCPA; in Colorado, rules of the attorney general.
notes.explanation: California's statute points to technical specifications set in regulations.
notes.source: California Consumer Privacy Act (Civ. Code 1798.100 et seq.), CPPA text effective 1 Jan. 2026, § 1798.135(b)(1), p. 16
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (California state website conditions of use)
notes.evidence: based on technical specifications set forth in regulations adopted pursuant to paragraph(19) of subdivision (a) of Section 1798.185

notes.front: Which of these laws expressly give a right to a portable copy of personal data: the CCPA, the VCDPA and the Colorado Privacy Act?
notes.back: All three: Virginia and Colorado as a portability right, and the CCPA through disclosures in a readily usable, transmissible format.
notes.explanation: The CCPA requires disclosures in a format that lets the consumer transmit the information to another entity.
notes.source: California Consumer Privacy Act (Civ. Code 1798.100 et seq.), CPPA text effective 1 Jan. 2026, § 1798.130(a)(2)(B), p. 11
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (California state website conditions of use)
notes.evidence: in a readily useable format that allows the consumer to transmit this information from one entity

notes.front: How does the scope of the opt-out right differ between the CCPA and the VCDPA?
notes.back: The CCPA's opt-out covers sale and sharing; Virginia's covers targeted advertising, sale and significant profiling.
notes.explanation: California's statute names its right 'the right to opt out of sale or sharing'.
notes.source: California Consumer Privacy Act (Civ. Code 1798.100 et seq.), CPPA text effective 1 Jan. 2026, § 1798.120(a)(1), p. 8
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (California state website conditions of use)
notes.evidence: This right may be referred to as the right to opt out of sale or sharing.

notes.front: How does the CPPA's approach to cure differ from Virginia's?
notes.back: Virginia's Attorney General must give 30 days' notice and a chance to cure; the CPPA may choose whether to allow a cure.
notes.explanation: For the CPPA, a cure period is a discretionary decision, not a precondition of action.
notes.source: California Consumer Privacy Act (Civ. Code 1798.100 et seq.), CPPA text effective 1 Jan. 2026, § 1798.199.45(a), p. 61
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (California state website conditions of use)
notes.evidence: The agency may decide not to investigate a complaint or decide to provide a business with a time period to cure the alleged violation.

notes.front: A business receives a CPPA complaint notice. It points out it never meant to break the law and had already fixed the problem. What may the CPPA consider?
notes.back: C: Lack of intent and voluntary cure efforts, in deciding whether to investigate or allow time to cure.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing: the CPPA must prosecute every complaint
B) Only the business's revenue
C) Lack of intent and voluntary cure efforts
D) Whether the Attorney General has also been told
notes.choicesExplained: A: the CPPA has discretion not to investigate. B and D: these are not the listed factors.
notes.explanation: These are the factors the statute lists for the CPPA's decision.
notes.source: California Consumer Privacy Act (Civ. Code 1798.100 et seq.), CPPA text effective 1 Jan. 2026, § 1798.199.45(a), p. 61
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (California state website conditions of use)
notes.evidence: (1) Lack of intent to violate this title. (2) Voluntary efforts undertaken by the business, service provider, contractor, or person to cure the alleged violation prior to being notified by the agency of the complaint.
